C001035.text: I have carefully reviewed Todd Blanche’s qualifications to be Attorney General. This includes his record and responses to questions from Senators at the Department of Justice Appropriations hearing, his confirmation hearing, and in the weeks that followed. While I believe Mr. Blanche is a capable lawyer, the Department of Justice has become increasingly political. Mr. Blanche has taken several actions that have further eroded the Department’s independence, and that is the basis for my vote to oppose his confirmation: Mr. Blanche approved an order to shield the President, his sons, and the family business from IRS audits, protections unavailable to other American taxpayers. He approved the creation of a $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund. He promised an anti-abortion organization that he would seek to prohibit the mailing of abortion medication to women nationwide. Under his leadership, the Department attempted to indict Senators Mark Kelly and Elissa Slotkin over their ill-advised, but constitutionally protected, videos encouraging resistance to unlawful orders. More than 1,200 former Department of Justice employees have opposed his nomination, arguing that he has undermined the institution. For these reasons, I will vote against this nomination.

It was a privilege to join thousands of shipbuilders, Navy leaders and personnel, local residents, and supporters at Bath Iron Works today for the christening of the future USS William Charette (DDG-130). This Bath-built ship is named in honor of Medal of Honor recipient Master Chief Hospital Corpsman William Charette. During the Korean War, Charette shielded a wounded Marine from an enemy grenade with his own body. Despite suffering facial wounds and shock from the blast, he improvised bandages from his clothing and continued treating wounded Marines under enemy fire. His actions were directly responsible for saving many lives. Through this ship, his courage, humility, and devotion to others will continue to inspire generations of sailors.

R to @SenatorCollins: Arleigh Burke-class destroyers form the backbone of the Navy’s surface fleet, and the men and women of Bath Iron Works make “Bath Built is Best Built” not just a slogan, but a way of life. Since 2020, I have been proud to secure more than $10.9 billion in Navy contract obligations related to DDG-51 destroyers and more than $1.2 billion for shipyard infrastructure improvements, wage enhancements, and workforce initiatives, including investments at BIW. I wish the future USS William Charette fair winds and following seas. May God always speed her safely home.

Today, the Senate HELP Committee voted to advance bipartisan legislation I introduced with Senators Tim Kaine and Lisa Murkowski to prevent the Department of Education from transferring critical offices responsible for special education and rehabilitative services, postsecondary education, elementary and secondary education, and Indian education to other federal agencies that lack the staff and expertise needed to execute their missions. One of the offices protected by our bill manages programs established under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, known as IDEA, that help meet the educational needs of more than 8 million children with disabilities. Moving this work to the Department of Health and Human Services fundamentally misunderstands the purpose of the Special Education program. It is focused primarily on students’ educational needs, not their health care needs. Every American, regardless of background or disability, deserves access to a quality public education. These important landmark programs must remain at the Department of Education, where Congress specifically placed them and where they belong.

B000490.text: This week, the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, appeared before the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government. During the hearing, I asked the Director about how Congress can be any clearer to ensure that the Trump Administration understands that once a funding bill is signed into law, the President is not allowed to change or second-guess the spending and withhold it due to policy or political differences. That is at the heart of Article 1 of the U.S. Constitution and why Congress also passed the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, when President Nixon tried to withhold funds that were already obligated according to the law.

This week, I asked the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, to explain how poorly planned cuts to the federal workforce last year have weakened services and protections upon which Americans rely. This includes the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, which is responsible for protecting America’s agriculture from invasive species and diseases. USDA-APHIS began mounting a vigorous response to the resurgence of New World Screwworm – a deadly parasite affecting livestock – in 2024. However, in early 2025, the Administration illegally fired workers and forced others to resign, causing over 25 percent of all USDA-APHIS employees to leave. USDA’s New World Screwworm prevention, monitoring, surveillance, and control efforts were halted. USDA had approved $378 million in prevention and control funding for sterile fly facilities in 2023 and 2024, yet the money went unspent when the new administration paused funding. This is extremely concerning to our ranchers, and this outbreak could drive the price of food even higher. Unfortunately, we continue to see the fallout of the blunt and ill-considered cuts to federal workers, from the return of New World Screwworm to the United States, to farmers showing up to closed or understaffed Farm Service Agency offices, to attacks on our nuclear safety programs putting national security at risk. I will continue to hold the White House accountable, as I did this week during the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government hearing with Mr. Vought.

It is with heartfelt sadness that I learned of the passing of my dear friend, and magnificent former colleague, Kay Granger of Fort Worth, Texas. Some simply hold the gavel – Kay demonstrated what it meant to wield it. Her life and career were defined by a remarkable legacy of firsts: the first woman to become Mayor of Fort Worth, the first Republican woman elected to Congress from Texas, the first woman to Chair the Appropriations Defense Subcommittee, and the first woman to lead House Republicans on the Appropriations Committee. Yet, Kay never rested in the remarkableness of each milestone – she was always ready for the next responsibility, the next challenge, and the next opportunity to serve. I admired Kay Granger the moment I met her. She carried herself with an unmistakable grace, but behind her regal appearance was a razor-sharp tenacity that commanded any room. Kay demanded respect, and she got it from everyone she ever interacted with. Whip-smart and Texas tough, she had a presence that could settle any debate with little more than a look. I was lucky enough to know her personally and professionally through our work serving together in Republican leadership. So, I can attest with firsthand knowledge that ‘Don’t mess with Texas’ was more than a motto when it came to Kay. I know it well because I lost to her when we both sought the chairmanship of the Appropriations Committee previously. After that, our friendship and mutual respect didn’t change for one another. In fact, she named me to be her Vice Chair. Her mentorship and guidance were large parts of my own committee journey and helped prepare me for the privilege of succeeding her as Chairman. On the Appropriations Committee, Kay was known as a fiscal conservative, a defense hawk, and a hard – but fair – negotiator. Ever proud of her Texas roots, Granger ferociously fought for the interests of the Lone Star State. Her colleagues on both sides of the aisle always respected her professionalism, her good humor, her unfailing civility, and her willingness to strike a deal. Indeed, she and the first woman to Chair the Appropriations Committee, Nita Lowey of New York, were fast friends. They were partners who set the gold standard of how to achieve bipartisan consensus. Their portraits above our dais today remind us of the example they set and the responsibility we inherit. I will miss my friend Kay Granger. She set an unmatched standard of excellence, civility, professionalism, and dedication to duty that few can match – and no one will ever exceed. My thoughts and prayers are with Kay’s family, friends, and many admirers. We have lost a great lioness of the House, and I have lost a dear friend to whom I shall always be indebted.

For 250 years, our great experiment has faltered, flourished, evolved, and progressed. The American experience is ever-changing and as diverse as the people who call this country home. But one thing has remained constant – the idea of America has always been a beacon of hope. Protecting this country and the ideals and values it was founded on takes work. Democracy is demanding. It takes dedication and principle. And it takes the resounding belief that upholding those ideals and values is worth the fight because America is bigger than any one person. Because liberty can only truly endure when it is paired with responsibility, virtue, and a commitment to put public good ahead of personal ambition. Today, we celebrate the moment when our founding fathers openly declared that creating this country, based in liberty, was a necessity in the face of tyranny. Their legacy is that leadership requires courage when it’s difficult, integrity when no one is watching, and a willingness to put country above self. We must remember that our duty is not merely to the next election, but to the next generation. That should be the challenge for all Americans as we look forward to another 250 years. From Massachusetts, where the fight for freedom first began, I wish you a happy 4th of July. God Bless America always, God Bless all who call her home, and God Bless our courageous men and women in uniform who continue the fight for liberty today.

On Monday, our office suffered an unimaginable loss. Chris Matthews, my District Outreach and Communications Director, passed away unexpectedly. If any one of you begin to lose faith in our country, remember Chris Matthews. Remember he was without question one of the Commonwealth’s sharpest political minds – a generational talent. Remember that he was more than a Congressional aide. He took the belief that through our actions we all can bring needed change and brought it with him on many interstate bus rides to canvas distant pivotal states and to the doors of the families he inspired. Remember through his example that public service is a genuinely noble vocation. As a trusted member of our office, he helped countless veterans, families, and those who could not advocate for themselves. Those of us privileged to have worked with him for over fifteen years will remember his laugh and his wry, often biting, humor – contrasting the way things are to the way they could be. I enjoyed visiting Twin Knobs Dairy & Action Farms in Douglas County this week with Kaleb and Erin Rodgers to see their multi-generational operation firsthand. The Rodgers family milks 180 dairy cows while also raising beef cattle, continuing a proud farming tradition that’s been built through years of hard work and dedication. Like so many family farms across Missouri, they’re working to pass this operation on to their son, Everett, and I was excited to hear their farm is on track to earn Missouri Century Farm recognition. Thanks to the Working Families Tax Cuts, farms like Twin Knobs can count on permanent 100% immediate expensing and a permanent small business deduction, making it easier to grow, hire, and stay profitable — so operations like theirs can be passed down to Everett and the next generation. That’s the kind of certainty family farms need to keep operating for generations to come, and I’ll keep fighting for policies that provide it.

F000466.text: I first met Doylestown’s own Allison Hamilton in Washington last October, when she joined us with The Nature Conservancy to discuss the conservation challenges facing our region. Since then, we have continued working together on several of the conservation priorities most important to our region. Chief among them is protecting the Delaware River. As Co-Chair of the Congressional Delaware River Watershed Caucus, I am leading the bipartisan effort to reauthorize and strengthen the Delaware River Basin Restoration Program—ensuring continued investments in cleaner water, restored habitats, and the local communities and economies that depend on a healthy river system. We are also working together to advance my bipartisan Safeguarding Endangered Species Act, which would overturn the Administration’s rollback of longstanding protections against habitat destruction that kills or injures threatened and endangered wildlife. The health of our environment is inseparable from the health, character, and prosperity of our communities. Allison’s local perspective, The Nature Conservancy’s expertise, and their continued partnership are indispensable to moving this work forward. Thank you to Allison and the entire TNC team for all you do for our community, our environment, and the natural resources entrusted to our care.

Join me in congratulating two outstanding young leaders from BSA Troop 71—Sam Killenbeck of Warrington and Andrew Sueta of Doylestown—on earning the rank of Eagle Scout! For his project, Sam partnered with Heritage Conservancy to design and construct four picnic tables at Lindsey Farm, including an ADA-compliant table that will help ensure visitors of all abilities can gather and enjoy this specials property. Andrew drew upon his love of American history to complete his project at the Bucks County Civil War Museum, constructing courtyard benches bookended by flower planters and creating a more welcoming setting for the outdoor presentations held there. What always stands out at a Court of Honor is that no Eagle Scout reaches this milestone alone. Speaking with Sam, Andrew, their fellow Scouts, troop leaders, friends, and families, you see the full strength of the Scouting community—young people choosing to work together and serve, and an entire village of support helping them turn that commitment into something lasting. Congratulations, Sam and Andrew—and thank you to the entire PA-1 Scouting family for continuing to lead through service!

I met with Edgely resident and former Bristol Township Mayor Sam Fenton as we continue our work to protect the historic Edgely riverfront community amid the proposed Delaware River Turnpike Bridge expansion. From the moment our residents brought these concerns to me, I have made clear to the PA Turnpike Commission and their partner agencies that infrastructure projects must never uproot families, disregard private property rights, or sacrifice the character of a deeply rooted neighborhood. Sam’s knowledge of Edgely, and his decades of public service, are critical as we continue pressing for every feasible alignment, design option, and construction plan to be fully examined before any family is impacted. Safe infrastructure and a protected Edgely community are not competing priorities. We can—and must—achieve both. I will continue standing with Edgely residents, demanding transparency and accountability, and ensuring their voices guide every decision that affects their homes, their property, and their future.

🚨 The Senate should not delay the SNAP state benefit cost-share requirement. States make more than $10 billion in erroneous SNAP payments every year, and the national payment error rate has nearly doubled since 2019. The problem is only getting worse. The One Big Beautiful Bill brings SNAP in line with other federally funded, state-administered programs, requiring states with the highest payment error rates to have skin in the game by sharing a modest portion of benefit costs. That's commonsense accountability, stronger program integrity, and better stewardship of taxpayer dollars. With our national debt exceeding $39 trillion, we must stay committed to fiscal responsibility—not cave to Democrat demands to weaken accountability, waste taxpayer dollars meant to serve vulnerable Americans, and further fuel our debt crisis.

Fun Fact Friday: As we celebrate the 250th anniversary of American independence, I want to highlight some of the signers of the Declaration of Independence. Richard Henry Lee was born in Virginia in 1732. At age 16, he sailed to England to continue his education. While he was studying in England, his parents died, leaving him an orphan. Returning to the colonies, Lee volunteered to raise a military company for the French and Indian War. In 1758, he was elected to the House of Burgesses. Seeking to serve his community, Lee applied to be a tax collector during the Stamp Act period. This led him to be censured and began his support for the cause for independence. While serving in the Second Continental Congress, he drafted what was known as the Lee Resolution that was used as guidance for the Declaration of Independence. He signed the Declaration in August of 1776.

I stopped by Branhilda Richardson Knowles Memorial Park in Deerfield Beach to pay respect to an important piece of our local history. I was proud to help secure funding for this park when I was a state legislator.   Born in the Bahamas, Branhilda Richardson Knowles came to Deerfield Beach in 1922 and served as a midwife for the African American community at a time when segregation denied many Black residents access to hospitals and other medical care.   The park that now bears her name also preserves a historic African American cemetery, where Black and Bahamian residents were buried during the Jim Crow era because they were prohibited from being laid to rest in the city cemetery.   Grateful to see how Deerfield Beach has worked to honor the people who helped build the community we know today.

On this day in history in 1926, master illusionist Harry Houdini was submerged underwater in an airtight metal casket after being challenged by rival magician Rahman Bey. It would take Houdini 91 minutes to escape. This was the final major stunt of a career filled with daring escapes and illusions. On this day in history in 1492, Christopher Columbus and his crew set sail for China and India on the Niña, Pinta, and Santa Maria. The ships reached land in the Bahamas a few months later before seeing Cuba, which Columbus assumed was China. After, he sighted Hispaniola, thinking it may be Japan. The crew returned to Spain with gold and spices. Columbus would make four expeditions to the Americas over the course of his lifetime. Columbus died in 1506 never realizing he founded the New World for Europe, which would help make Spain the wealthiest country on Earth for a century.

Welles Crowther, a volunteer firefighter from Nyack and an equities trader working in the World Trade Center, jumped into action when the attacks occurred. He could have escaped the South Tower. Wearing the red bandana his father had given him as a boy, he became forever known as the “Man in the Red Bandana” - a symbol of courage, selflessness, and the very best of America. The Presidential Medal of Freedom cannot repay what Welles gave, but it ensures that his extraordinary bravery and sacrifice will never be forgotten. M001228.text: RT by @RepMaloyUtah: On Pioneer Day, I had the opportunity to tour Beaver and see firsthand the devastating impact of both wildfire and flooding. Standing in those burned and flooded landscapes, talking with the Forest Service personnel, local leaders, and the people of Beaver one thing was crystal clear: forest management works. The difference between treated and untreated forest was visible. Areas that had been thinned or otherwise managed gave firefighters a chance. They slowed the fire, reduced its intensity, helped crews establish containment lines, and in some cases, stopped the fire altogether. In the overgrown, untreated areas, the fire burned hotter, moved faster, and left behind far greater destruction, burning an unprecedented 70,000 acres in two days. It's frustrating that while the United States is the world's largest importer of lumber and paper products, millions of acres of our own forests sit overcrowded and vulnerable to catastrophic wildfire. The boots-on-the-ground Forest Service personnel managing these forests know what needs to be done and want to actively manage these lands, but too often commonsense projects are delayed or stopped by endless litigation and opposition by environmentalists and bureaucrats in Washington D.C. That's why the Fix Our Forests Act deserves to move forward. The legislation passed the House with strong bipartisan support, but has been stalled in the Senate for 18 months. It needs to move forward. I'm grateful to Congresswoman Celeste Maloy for bringing us together to see this firsthand, and to the Trump Administration officials who came to Utah to witness these conditions on the ground. With the U.S. Forest Service headquarters coming to Utah, we have a tremendous opportunity to ensure the people making decisions about our forests are closer to the landscapes and communities they serve. Thank you to USDA's Michael Boren, Sam Crofts from the Bureau of Land Management, and Chairman Bruce Westerman of the House Natural Resources Committee for taking the time to be there and hear directly from those who have been impacted by this catastrophe. On Pioneer Day weekend, that lesson feels especially meaningful. The pioneers who settled this state understood that stewardship requires hard work, planning, and taking responsibility for the land we call home. We honor their legacy not by leaving our forests untouched until they burn and cause catastrophic damage, but by actively caring for them so they remain healthy for generations to come. The Beaver community continues to show incredible resilience. I was reminded why I'm so proud to be a Utahn. We face challenges head-on, we help our neighbors, and we don't shy away from doing the difficult work that's necessary to protect our communities and our public lands. @realDonaldTrump @RepMaloyUtah @RepWesterman @SenJohnCurtis @RepBurgessOwens @RepMikeKennedy @USDA @forestservice @Interior @BLMNational @NatResources @JStuartAdams @cralbrecht52 @BeaverCountyUT

ROAD TO 250: The Road to Independence Semper Paratus! As we continue to mark America's 250th anniversary, we celebrate the institutions that helped build our young nation. On August 4, 1790, Secretary of the Treasury Alexander Hamilton established the Revenue Marine, the forerunner of today's U.S. Coast Guard. Created just one year after the First Congress established the Treasury Department, it was one of the first federal services of the new republic, charged with enforcing tariff laws and protecting the nation's maritime commerce. Today, the @USCG —our nation's premier maritime service—includes nearly 42,000 active-duty men and women who protect our maritime borders, ensure the safe and lawful flow of commerce, conduct search and rescue missions, and save lives. Their mission is strengthened by dedicated Reservists and nearly 26,000 volunteers serving in the U.S. Coast Guard Auxiliary. On the U.S. Coast Guard's 236th birthday, we thank the men and women of the U.S. Coast Guard—including those serving in Sectors New York and Long Island Sound—for their unwavering commitment to protecting our communities and our nation. Semper Paratus!

We discussed the tremendous potential of the Kodiak Spaceport Complex, one of the nation's critical commercial launch sites, as well as Poker Flat Research Range outside of Fairbanks, the world's only university-owned rocket range and a cornerstone of atmospheric and space research.   As investment in aerospace continues to grow, we have an incredible opportunity to prepare Alaska's students, engineers and technicians for high-paying careers right here at home. By strengthening partnerships with NASA, our universities, our military installations, and the private sector, we can ensure Alaska remains a key player in space innovation.   I appreciate Administrator Isaacman taking the time to discuss our shared vision and look forward to working together to ensure Alaska continues to serve as a vital launch point for discovery and as a key component in our nation's space leadership strategy.

I was honored to welcome my friend, the Ambassador of Hungary to the United States, @_SzabolcsTakacs to Haralson County today. In the late 1800s, dozens of Hungarian families moved from Pennsylvania's coal mines to Haralson County to establish a wine-making community.  They named their village Budapest after the Hungarian capital, and planted vineyards across the surrounding hillsides.  After Prohibition was enacted in the 1920s, many of the families left, and all that remains from that era is a home which once served as a Catholic rectory and the historic Budapest cemetery.  Today, we visited both. Ambassador Takács' visit is a special moment in Haralson County's rich history, and I am grateful for the incredible support the Haralson County Historical Society, the Hungarian Community Church of Georgia, the Dogwood Hills team, and local officials and community leaders provided to facilitate this meaningful event. Thank you, Ambassador Takács, for visiting Georgia's 3rd Congressional District, and thank you for strengthening the relationship between Hungary and the United States of America! @HungaryinUSA

RT by @RepBrianJack: Grateful to join the amazing Steve Gradick of WLPP and @RepBrianJack in Carrollton, Georgia yesterday for a fun long chat on all things America, agriculture, and saving our country. We announced the finalized Cooperative Interstate Shipment (CIS) agreement, giving qualifying Georgia state-inspected meat processors the opportunity to ship USDA-labeled products across state lines. This is a tremendous victory for Georgia's farmers, ranchers, and small meat processors. Yesterday, Georgia became one of only a handful of states participating in the Cooperative Interstate Shipment Program—allowing qualifying state-inspected meat processors to ship USDA-labeled products nationwide. For too long, a handful of massive processors have dominated the market, putting family-owned processors at a disadvantage. This is another step toward expanding opportunity, strengthening rural America, increasing competition, and rebuilding America's food production capacity. Under Biden, the United States flipped from net agricultural exporter to net importer. Four years of weakness turned a historic American strength into a strategic vulnerability. We’re fixing that. Food security is national security. Thank you Georgia!!! 🥩🐂🇺🇸

Face à la situation migratoire à Ceuta, j’ai été en contact avec le Président du gouvernement espagnol pour marquer notre solidarité et proposer toute aide nécessaire, y compris via Frontex. Je salue la coopération en cours avec le Maroc, qui a déjà permis aujourd’hui plus de 40 000 retours de Ceuta vers le Maroc. Les ministres de l’Intérieur sont en contact pour assurer un suivi étroit de la situation. Ceuta ne bénéficie pas de la libre circulation vers le reste de l’espace Schengen. J’ai toutefois demandé dès hier au Ministre de l’Intérieur de renforcer les contrôles à notre frontière avec l’Espagne si cela devait être nécessaire : 4 unités de forces mobiles, des avions et des drones sont déployés. Ces mesures viennent renforcer les dispositions que nous avons prises depuis 2020 pour mieux protéger notre frontière avec l’Espagne en étroite coordination, avec des brigades communes et une action conjointe de lutte contre l’immigration clandestine. Ces mesures viennent compléter les instruments européens adoptés pour assurer les retours et appliquer le pacte asile et migrations, avec 25% de chute des flux irréguliers vers l’Union européenne l’an dernier et une baisse poursuivie sur les routes migratoires atlantique et de Méditerranée occidentale en 2026. Solidarité et responsabilité avec nos partenaires européens pour faire appliquer nos règles de fermeté en matière de retours et de protection des frontières extérieures de l’Union. Je redis ici notre solidarité à l’Espagne, son gouvernement et son peuple.
